I was not a member of the transport committee when this bill was being considered, but having looked at the proceedings one of the most glaring omissions appears to be that there was no evidence at all adduced before the committee with respect to transportation by air, both of a private and of a commercial character. The second most glaring omission is that there does not appear to have been any evidence at all with respect to transportation in the northern areas of our country.
Sitting here listening to various members speak about transportation problems and the ramifications of the provisions of this bill, it struck me, as it often strikes me, that the members who sit here-I say this not unkindly-tend to confine their mental projections from St. John's, Newfoundland to Victoria on Vancouver Island.
[DOT] (6:30 p.m.)
They fail to appreciate the great need for north-south communication in this country, and for internal communication facilities above the sixtieth parallel as well as in the northern portions of provinces. The only reference in some 3,000 pages of testimony that I can find to air transport is that contained in a brief submitted by the Canadian Pacific. At pages 31 and 32 of the brief, they refer to a legitimate complaint not dealt with by the bill before us. The complaint should be dealt with by placing Air Canada under the same authority that other carriers are placed under. The bill before us brings transport by air, as the Canadian Pacific brief points out-to which the Aeronautics Act applies-under the jurisdiction of the new Canadian commission. The Aeronautics Act applies equally to all carriers except Air Canada. On an application for a licence Air Canada need not establish that the service is and will be required for the present and future public convenience and
(Mr. Saltsman.l
necessity. Its licence cannot be made the subject of the controls and conditions applied to licences granted to other carriers. In effect, the Governor in Council is the individual, with the Minister of Transport-not the Air Transport Board-controlling the domestic routes operated by Air Canada and the conditions under which they shall be operated.
Once Air Canada has made an agreement under section 15 or 24 of the Trans-Canada Air Lines Act with the Minister of Transport, it can make application to the board and the board is required to grant to Air Canada a licence under such terms and subject to such conditions as will enable Air Canada to perform the agreement. It seems to me that Canadian Pacific makes a valid point in its brief to the transport committee. The bill should direct itself to matters such as I have mentioned rather than dealing, as it does, with amending the Aeronautics Act for purposes of bringing dry leases on aircraft under the control of the board.
I, too, am fearful of the tremendous power to be given to this new commission with respect to one of the most vital segments of our country's economy. The Minister of Transport said he was very much in favour of the kind of parliamentary control suggested by the hon. member for Peace River, and the amendment the hon. member proposed yesterday. I was happy to hear what was said. The government is becoming more and more complex as the world takes on the complexities of the space age. This is no excuse to carve out of segments of public affairs concerning the people as a whole, great chunks of administrative authority and turning them over to what inevitably must become bureaucratic control. There are many shortcomings adopted in the methods of the Air Transport Board in dealing with the myriads of questions coming before it, with the only appeal being to the minister. Regardless of how valid an application might be for the beginning of a commercial air service, for instance, there is no appeal from the decision of the Air Transport Board. Almost invariably, the board bases its decision on evidence taken at public hearings before an individual who is not even a member of the board.
Counsel or assistant counsel hold hearings which are sometimes of great length, listening to volumes of evidence as to the public interest. Then, because of the routine adopted with respect to the internal management of the
December 21, 1966

affairs of the Air Transport Board, the individual hearing evidence presents a brief either in written or verbal form to the board. It is on the basis of that kind of information that decisions yea or nay are made.
What will happen? Under the bill there will be set up various committees or subcommittees of the Canadian Transportation Commission. One of those committees will deal with matters affecting air transport in the country. A provision of the bill ensures that the chairman of the Air Transport Board, whoever he may be at the time of the coming into force of this act, will be the chairman of that subcommittee. Over him and over all the other committees will be the chairman of the commission, who, in effect, will be the czar of Canadian transport of all kinds over which the government of Canada has jurisdiction.
This is a tremendous responsibility and tremendous power to put into the hands of an individual. Such administrative control cannot be abdicated by the parliament of Canada, by those of us sitting here representing the people by due process. The immediate word coming to mind, when looking at legislation such as this is Lord Hewart's new despotism. Such will be the inevitable role that this commission will play in affairs of transportation in this country.
Some sort of appeal procedure seems to have been written into this legislation. An appeal simply to the minister, as exists in the present Air Transport Board routine, is insufficient, notwithstanding that with his usual benevolence the minister probably views all such appeals with that impartiality for which he is noted. How does the bill affect air transport generally? The committee proceedings, as I have said, said nothing about this except for two pages in the brief produced by the Canadian Pacific.
[DOT] (6:40 p.m.)
The announcement which the minister made to the house on October 20 of regional air carrier policy deals with every phase of air transportation except one. It deals with the two main line carriers in Canada. It deals very briefly with commercial charter operations, but says nothing about general aviation. Notwithstanding the fact that we had recent amendments to the Aeronautics Act, the new despotism is still sniping at an area of aviation which made aviation possible in this country, indeed made Canada a leader in aviation matters throughout the world.
Transportation
I refer to clause 93 of the bill. If it is passed as it stands it will make every person who is the owner of an aircraft, and who desires to lease it, subject to obtaining first the approval of the Canadian transport commission, or the subcommittee on air. This is an entirely undue restriction. I speak not simply because I happen to be found in a personal position here. Many people in general aviation throughout this country acquire aircraft and are able to do so because of the probability of being able to lease them on a dry lease basis.
I know there are lots of bootlegging operations of frustrated air carriers who purchase aircraft simply for the purpose of getting into the business and lease them to licensed air carriers. But when you pass a blanket provision, such as this amendment which is prepared to the Aeronautics Act, you are catching all the little people who happen to own aircraft.
The minister has been a champion, certainly while he has been Minister of Transport and I have no reason to believe that his philosophy was ever any different, of protecting the government air line, Air Canada, at all costs. In my view, this has worked to the disadvantage of air progress in Canada. I am sure he is aware of the editorials that have been written with respect to his policies, both past and present. When he announced in 1964 a segment of his air policy, he said that in the domestic field any development of competition should not compromise or seriously injure the economic viability of T.C.A. main line domestic operations which represent the essential framework of its domestic network services. In other words, he said there must not be the kind of competition which would put T.C.A. into the red.
The minister nods his head that this is right. I disagree with the minister, as have many editorial writers. I submit to him that this is not true Liberalism when he adopts this kind of philosophy, because it completely negates the philosophy of free competition. The air line that is going to survive will be that one that can compete efficiently and economically, and that is what a mass of editorials have pointed out.
The minister has said that the policy on regional services calls for a reasonable role for regional air carriers, which will give the regional air carriers a reasonable chance to operate without government subsidies. He used the word "reasonable" twice, and that indicates the extent to which the minister feels there must be that degree of control

December 21, 196S
Transportation
which will ensure that there will not be any degree of competition which would have the effect of putting Air Canada into the red, no matter what kind of operation it may be, efficient or otherwise.
An editorial from a Saskatchewan newspaper commented as follows:
Whenever a government determines on a policy which necessarily involves subsidization, this amounts to an increased direct tax on individual Canadians. In this reference, competition-which means less not more government intrusion in business and industry-is the only certain safeguard the taxpayer has against extravagant policy-making.
That is the view which has been generally expressed with regard to this concept of the minister's.
I notice in the guide lines of the government respecting regional air carrier policy that he tabled in the house on October 20, he has dwelt at length on the relationship of Air Canada with not only C.P.A. but other regional carriers. With respect to routes, route transfers and the division of routes between the two national carriers he said that some anomalies exist and more may develop as a result of future growth with respect to these divisions.
I suggest that when these guide lines were being prepared, the minister had no real regard or concentrated concern about the north-en portions of the provinces and northern Canada generally. If ever there were areas in which there must be a far-sighted attitude developed toward the provision of transportation facilities, it is in those areas.
I can recall the minister's attitude when he was on this side of the house when it was suggested that a rail line be constructed to Pine Point. He and his supporters of the day joined together and voted against that. Now, of course, they clutch it to their bosoms as though it were their own idea, and a good thing. The minister of northern affairs was not present when the vote was taken on that matter, and so he can now feel free to say a very laudable thing was done in the construction of that railway, an operation that was paid for far earlier than was ever anticipated even by the proposers of the legislation at that time.
Similar developments are now taking place in the Yukon, the Northwest Territories and the northern portions of the provinces. I am sure the minister of northern affairs has acquainted the Minister of Transport of the tremendous development taking place in the Yukon where rail facilities are going to be

necessary. The government has caused a survey to be made, paid for jointly by it and by the private concern that is interested in developing the ore in the area, but these developments will not come about unless transportation facilities are provided there.
What consideration does this bill give to the nagging problem of the barrier of the panhandle of Alaska cutting off, as it does, a great portion of the coast of British Columbia and the entire Yukon Territory? We have a copper mine coming into production next spring in the Yukon, New Imperial Mines Ltd., with a long-term contract for the supply of copper to world markets.
The normal docking facilities on the panhandle, on United States territory 105 miles away, are not adequate. It is now discovered that the ore will have to be brought from its place of production all the way to Vancouver in order to be trans-shipped to world markets, even though tide water is only 105 miles away.
[DOT] (6:50 p.m.)
All we get from the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development is studies, studies and more studies. We are being snowed under by studies. The same number of studies will be undertaken now with regard to that problem as have been, and likely will be, undertaken with regard to the provision of a paved route between Alaska and continental United States. 1 do not particularly blame the members of this government any more than I blame the vast majority of the members who sit in this house for not being oriented geographically to the fact that there exists this vast area and this vast potential in the northern part of our country. Were it not for the transportation costs which form the major factor in respect of any decision which would bring a new development to fruition in the north, there would be all sorts of economic development in this part of Canada.
The richest silver mine in North America now is closing because the costs have risen to the stage now where they no longer can continue to compete in world markets. The biggest single factor in the cost of producing that product is transportation. Then there is the living cost. If hon. members believe that costs are skyrocketing here in the south, they would not need to pause very long in reflection to realize what the transportation cost for 1,500 miles from the port of Vancouver to White Horse means in relation to the additional cost of everything used in the north. When we have to carefully consider and
December 21, 1966

think twice before we order an extra package of insulation because it costs more to transport that 1,500 miles than it does to transport a pound of butter and such things, then we have some small insight into the over-all problem. Everything that reaches us costs more.
I do not think that subsidies are the answer. I do not think the subsidies which were suggested in the air policy that the minister tabled last October are the answer. If there were a more enlightened view taken in respect of allowing competitive services to generate in these areas, that well might provide the answer. If the government would get out of such operations as Eldorado aviation and allow private enterprise to fill the gap-which it can do and which it has assured the government it can do-that might be part of the answer. Then of course, there always is the government's obligation to provide surface means of transportation in the form of highways and railways.
Instead of sniping away, as clause 93 of this bill does-and I am only picking on clause 93 because it is an indication of what is happening and how the freedom of the individual is being eroded by this sort of direction-what the government should be doing in respect of the provision of adequate incentives to the development of aviation in the country is paying perhaps a little less attention to the Canadian main line and major regional carriers in the country and a little more attention to general aviation, which after all was the birth place of what the minister now is so proud of, Air Canada.
General aviation is being put in a strait-jacket of rules and regulations which stifles the growth of this segment of the air industry. One example of this is that it is contrary to the air regulations to land or take off at an unlicensed air strip. It is a recognized fact that aircraft are being used more and more in the agricultural industry in this country. Aircraft are being used by the farmers. Yet, if he takes off and lands on a strip which is not licensed or which is on his farm, he is guilty of an offence. Of course there always are the over-zealous police officers who come along and lay charges. Under the regulations as they now exist this farmer would be guilty of an offence by flying under 500 feet when he was landing or taking off from his unlicensed airstrip. He may be engaged in spraying his crop, counting his cattle, or looking over his land in the spring preparatory to seeding. A very excellent television film about the part aircraft
Transportation
are playing in respect of the agricultural industry was shown last week end.
This type of niggardly regulation should be done away with. Instead of looking for more ways to restrict the growth of aviation in this country, the government and the officials of the Department of Transport should be looking for sections which they could take out in order to make it a little easier for private aviation to grow in this country.
Another good example of the way in which the healthy growth of aviation is being stifled in this country is the airport policy which does not allow convenient usage of private airplanes. I was in the city of Vancouver where persons wishing to use a private aircraft sometimes must wait until half a dozen other airplanes are pulled out of the way before they can take off. The reason for this is that the Department of Transport, by its policies, will not allow the construction and placement of "T" hangars such as the one now in use at Uplands airport. There is no earthly reason that this policy should not be changed so as to allow this kind of convenience for those who are in a position to take advantage of it.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR DEFINITION AND IMPLEMENTATION OF NATIONAL POLICY
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I did not expect that I would have an opportunity to speak on this bill. I have, however, been very interested in reading it. I should have liked to have had the opportunity to participate in the work of the committee which gave consideration to this bill. I believe only the Minister of Transport could have designed a bill which starts out with a very clearly defined policy and then arrives at as many "ifs", "ands", and "buts" as this bill has. The bill indicates that there cannot be any real transportation policy. This really is not a transportation bill, as I had envisaged it a number of years ago when I moved a resolution suggesting that we have a national transportation policy.
[DOT] (7:00 p.m.)
I have long been concerned with many parts of the problem in Canada which relates to a national transportation policy. I was particularly interested in the shenanigans which took place in connection with the railways and the public attitude toward those railways. There are those who say that the Canadian National is a crown company and that the people of Canada own it. I do not think this is true; we do not own it. It is a little like the

December 21, 1966
Transportation
case of the man who pays $10 on a new car and finds himself with a $10,000 debt. It is much similar to what is said about the Canadian National. We pay so much interest on its debt it is doubtful that we can say the C.N.R. is a government agency owned by the Canadian people. It would be more logical for those operating the C.N.R. to fit its operations to the needs of the public. They should provide leadership in the field of transportation. From my own experience I can say that in the field of public relations the Canadian National, so far as transportation of passengers and goods is concerned, is no more interested in the welfare of this country than a number of other railway companies. In fact some others in many ways serve the public better.
It is foolish for the government to suggest that a national transportation policy should be adopted, such as the one outlined in th s bill, if this whole problem is not faced, and I refer to the duplication of lines by the C.N.R. and the C.P.R. In my area there has been talk about abandoning a line. Yet people working for the railway have said that the cost of repairs in recent years warrants the operation of the line, without any increase in the volume of business, for a considerable period of time. There is a potential increase in transportation need in this same area as a result of the development of natural resources, but the railway company continues to threaten abandonment of this line.
Surely it is foolish to have two railway companies operating duplicate services across this country, competing in areas where competition is of no value. Railways in certain areas should be considered as public utilities and there is an advantage to the public in owning these facilities. With the advent of the block system, with one dispatcher controlling all the trains in a division, it would seem reasonable to operate these two lines as one. The minister will eventually have to face up to the necessity of public ownership of this public utility.
An hon. member suggested it would be to the advantage of Canada to place both railway companies on a free enterprise basis. If we do not combine them and operate them as a public utility perhaps that would be advantageous and would lead to a solution of our transportation problem. The railway companies admit they are facing a problem which they will not be able to solve even with the limited freedom provided by this bill.

I am always bothered when the C.N.R. comes to parliament for more money, particularly when I think of its inefficient operations and the waste it incurs without satisfying the needs of the people it serves. I remember when I first came to Ottawa in 1957. At that time one could get a berth on a train running from here to northern Ontario. Anyone who had a little money could get an upper berth. Someone with more money could get a roomette, and someone with even more money could get a drawing room or a bedroom. Very soon after the railway company decided to stop sleeping car services at En-glehart. Th s meant that people travelling from northern Ontario to Montreal had to get up very early in the morning at Englehart and travel the remainder of the distance by coach.
Not very long after that it was decided that sleeping car accommodation should be abandoned at North Bay. People travelling to or from th:s area had to make special arrangements in order to obtain sleepers. All this took place at a time when the railway companies purchased sleeping cars from the New York Central Railway at $10,000 per car. Those cars may well have been satisfactory for operation in southern Ontario but they were not satisfactory on this line. On occasion one would find the left side of a car completely frozen up while at the same time the temperature on the other side of the car was about 100 degrees. After discovering this fact I found out that the C.N.R. was charging the province of Ontario $250 per month to keep these sleepers on this line in northern Ontario. Presumably it did not take the C.N.R. very long to pay for the cost of these cars.
Obviously these companies were and are not interested in passenger service. An example of this is the fact that trains going to northern Ontario and northern Quebec met at stations at about two o'clock in the morning. They did not depart until four hours later. During the interval the passengers waited in cold stations. I remember leaving Ottawa on numerous occasions to catch a train which was supposed to depart at 10.55. After several such trips I arrived no earlier than 1.30 a.m., only to find that I was approximately an hour early.
a (7:10 p.m.)
I was very surprised when I went there one day to find that the train had gone. One of the chaps at the station said it had left at the regular time. That night it left about 11.30. The railway had made the service so bad that obviously nobody was travelling on the train.
December 21, 1966

Then it went before the board and asked permission to drop the Continental, a train that travelled from Montreal to the west coast. The railway dropped it. I invite hon. members to travel from northern Ontario to Ottawa or Montreal by train. They will find that you get to North Bay at about twelve o'clock and the other train arrives any time after two o'clock. The minister may smile, but this is how the Canadian National operates. The connecting train was so late that, not having anything to do in North Bay and not particularly wanting to sit in the station all night, I stayed on the other train, went to Toronto, had my breakfast in Toronto, spent two hours there and caught the train from there to Ottawa which was held up here at the Beach-burg siding for five or ten minutes while the train from North Bay passed through on its way to Ottawa. In the meantime I have travelled half way around Ontario to fill in the time. The railways have not been interested in passenger traffic.
Then there is the question of freight. I was interested to learn that nobody in my area ships cows by rail. If under the community sales system they ship cows by rail to Toronto, a distance of about 350 miles, it takes anywhere from two to four days for the cows to reach Toronto. Anyone who ships cattle knows the cost involved in feeding and watering them, taking them off the cars and putting them back on again, and the fact that there is four days' shrinkage in the cows also has to be taken into consideration. This is a very expensive way of moving cattle to Toronto. These people can ship their cows from the community sales barns in New Liskeard and Earlton at night and they will be in Toronto the next morning and on the market that day. I have asked the railway why they cannot provide this type of service. They admit that they could but say they are not going to bother because it would take some planning and they would have to make arrangements they had not previously considered making.

speechtext: We are not really involved in public ownership. The Canadian National Railways are not publicly owned.

speechtext: Oh, oh.

speechtext: We bought it but we have never paid for it. The minister can laugh. Just let him look it up.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR DEFINITION AND IMPLEMENTATION OF NATIONAL POLICY
speechtext: We have been paying for it for years.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR DEFINITION AND IMPLEMENTATION OF NATIONAL POLICY
speechtext:
We have been paying for it ever since the Grand Trunk went bankrupt. We are still paying for it. We do not repay anything on the principal; we are having enough trouble paying the interest. We do not own it. We might as well be renting the damn thing. This is also true of some things in the ownership of the Ontario government.
If we are to have a truly national transportation system we will have to relate it to the needs of the people and provide a satisfactory service. The minister can laugh. We can put any public utility out of business if we wish to do so. We can slow down or stop any train operating if we wish to do so. All we have to do is make the facility so bad that it does not satisfy the needs of the people using it. We have done that very well in the cases I have cited as examples.
As I see it, this policy is not going to help the situation one bit. We are trying to relate the problems that face us to Canadian Pacific and Canadian National without really helping either company to solve them. Before we really solve the problems in this area we have to provide a utility that is publicly owned and controlled and will be used for the advantage of Canada. We the people of Canada are willing to make the necessary contribution in the way of subsidies.
I do not think the situation has changed since the days when the bridge principle was introduced. I do not believe there is really any objection to the subsidies we provide for those areas that cannot carry the facility. In my opinion we have to try to get some advantage out of the facilities that are provided. Revenue must be obtained from them. Only recently have the railways given any consideration to some of these problems. Canadian National and Canadian Pacific recently made a deal whereby Canadian Pacific would get out of the transportation field in the Ottawa area. What has happened since this arrangement was brought about? We now have trains running from Toronto to Ottawa and Toronto to Montreal which are providing a reasonable

December 21, 1966
Transportation
service. For the first time we are finding that the people of Canadian National are proud to talk about their Rapido train. This is no advance in railroading; this type of transportation has been provided in Canada for years. I can remember when the Silver Bullet of New York Central travelled through Canada with one stop at St. Thomas. That train averaged over 80 miles an hour; on a number of occasions it averaged over 90 miles an hour.
We now find the Canadian National, 20 years later, bragging about the fact that they have the most rapid transportation system on the continent. This type of facility was present in Canada for a number of years, sort of in bondage, but it was there for Canadians to examine and find out how transportation could be made profitable. As long as we are not willing to face the problem of Canadian National and Canadian Pacific and their relationship, as long as we are willing to call for competition between them, this bill will not provide the type of national transportation policy that the government suggests it will provide.
Other problems will have to be faced more realistically than they are today. This bill is a catch-all to the extent that the government has introduced a completely new category of transportation and has literally thrown it in with the National Energy Board. We will have to face this problem because it relates to the railroads and their ability to produce economically. I refer to commodity pipe lines. There is on the order paper now a bill involving the Shell Oil Company and the building of a small pilot, research pipe line at a cost of approximately $50 million. The company hopes that this commodity pipe line will carry sulphur, 1 believe, from Saskatchewan to its refinery on the coast.
I think we should be quite happy to support it in its desire to develop this facility, which has been used in other countries. It means that through the medium of oil as the carrier they will be able to move the vast supplies of sulphur, potash and gypsum that are being found on the prairies and are now being hauled by the railroads. This is a new form of transportation that will create as much havoc as the railroad freight differentials, tariffs and the advent of trucking facilities, particularly trucking facilities which are under the control of the railroads and are competing with the railroads for similar types of freight carriage.
Under this bill these lines are classed as combined lines. Even the government could not make up its mind whether they would be

commodity-handling capsules, sludge carriers or lines handling commodities transmission. In recent days we have had some experience of pipe lines, as has the government. This experience will probably indicate whether the National Energy Board should control the licensing and handling of the transmission of commodities by pipe lines. Our experience indicates that the National Energy Board's operations in licensing and controlling the transmission of commodities owned or bought by companies should be governed by the national transportation policy.
[DOT] (7:20 p.m.)
Pipe lines will play a very important part in the future. In England it has been found that coal can be moved by pipe line. Experiments have been conducted in the use of pipe lines for the movement of capsules and packaged freight. According to the developments outlined in the submission by Shell Oil, I am sure that Canada will lead in the movement of many commodities through this medium. Of course this means that the miles and miles of box cars which one sees travelling across the prairies may eventually come to an end. It may be possible to transport grain and other commodities such as sulphur, gypsum and potash by this new transportation medium, and this will have a direct bearing on the volume of business undertaken by the railroads.
I think a saving could be affected if the government would think in terms of the public ownership of rail transportation facilities because I believe that there is a vast duplication of services in this area. It seems that the Canadian Pacific Railway wishes neither to continue nor to discontinue passenger service. It appears to be a dog in the manger in this field. If the C.P.R. were to say that it will upgrade its passenger service and let the C.N.R. out of that service, then I think the government would be well advised to consider such a proposition. However, I think it is possible for the two railways to provide the kind of service which the Canadian public should have and to do so economically through competition between the two railways which are operating side by side.
It is a fact that the C.P.R. has tried to discontinue certain lines. I remember comparing C.P.R. and C.N.R. fares for the same kind of accommodation on the North Bay-Ottawa run. I found that the C.P.R. rate was three times as high as the C.N.R. rate. This is an indication of Canadian Pacific's interest in that service. It is also an indication of the
December 21, 1966



non-existence of competition between these two companies because obviously the Canadian Pacific had increased the fares so as to discourage passengers from using its service. I am sure that considerable discussion will take place on some of these clauses but I believe that our attention should be drawn mainly to clause 1 because it seems to me that in the preamble of this bill the minister has expressed the hopes and aspirations of every member of parliament to define and implement a national transportation policy.
I think also that hon. members are concerned about the operation of highway transportation and the role it plays. I am referring both to C.N. transportation and to the subsidy we pay for C.P. freight as well as the role played by independent transport in this particular field. It is certain that the advent of increased shipping on the St. Lawrence seaway must be considered in relation to transportation. I am aware of the argument recently advanced in the house regarding the closing of the ports on the lower St. Lawrence river and the fact that this plays a considerable role in the freight costs and the movement of goods through the ports in the maritimes. I am also aware of the responsibility which the government must bear with regard to those ports and to communities dependent on the facilities that are provided. I believe that the general public is aware of the fact that these problems will not be solved with the passing of the bill.
I know that the hour is late and that the possibility of the minister commenting tonight on some of the major problems is remote. However, I should like to ask him to give the house a reasoned explanation of why the government will not consider the nationalization of the Canadian Pacific Railway Company so as to make possible the integration of the two railway companies and eliminate what I am sure the minister will agree is excessive duplication. Even in their present operations the railways are attempting to eliminate some of this duplication. Not long ago a matter was dropped from the order paper relating to the operations of an independent distributor for the express and freight sections of both railways in the Ottawa area. The railways tried to make an arrangement whereby these services could be integrated so that only one truck would make the deliveries from both railways instead of having two separate services. This duplication extends throughout the whole system. I think everyone here would agree that great savings could be effected if 23033-7271

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, looking closely at the bill I have realized that it arises out of the recommendations of the MacPherson royal commission. In a sense it is born out of that commission. The hon. member for Winnipeg South pointed out earlier today that the atmosphere in railroading today has changed. The minister admitted this in the committee and I could quote his own words. The railroads admit this too. The C.P.R. and C.N.R. have admitted that the atmosphere that brought about the establishment of the MacPherson royal commission has changed greatly between then and now.
In 1959 the atmosphere was depressing; the railroads were in financial difficulties. Today the opposite is true. Railroading has been given a tremendous boost by the recent huge grain shipments, by the development of the potash industry in Saskatchewan, by the iron ore mining developments in the Peace River country and by the development of the Pine Point railway, which we brought about and which the minister voted against. The hon. member for Winnipeg South went into this
[Mr. Pickersgill.l
fully and I will not repeat what he said, but I think it should be pointed out that the shippers or consumers initially brought about the MacPherson commission. The commission was appointed to look into their complaints.
The commission was asked to look into the inequities in the freight rate structure, their incidence upon the various regions of Canada, and the legislative and other changes that could and should be made in furtherance of national economic policy to remove or alleviate such inequities. One could interpret these terms very broadly, and the commission did. They even studied the Crowsnest pass rates, and I think in a sense studied them for too long.
In opening his remarks yesterday the minister said something about the railroads being the backbone of Canada. He then went on to say that their bony structure must be healthy. By that statement and by his statements in the committee he has shown he is vitally concerned about the financial position of the railroads. This is why I ask why the royal commission was set up in the first place. It was set up to iron out some of the inequities experienced by consumers or shippers in the matter of freight rates.
What did the British Columbia government say in their brief to the committee? They said:
We must conclude that the recommendations of the royal commission in regard to inequities in the freight rate structure are not reflected in Bill C-231.
In other words, Bill C-231 does not answer what the royal commission was set up to study.
The brief goes on:

I thought this was a rather weak argument because no one believes that the freeze placed on the railroads in 1959 and the subsidy paid because of it should go on forever. But if a freeze was considered necessary in 1959, so necessary that it was acceptable to parliament and the country, how can one readily accept a bill which says, Take the freeze off and let everything go? How can one accept those two principles? This is where the minister's argument was weak.
Certainly we agree that legislation is necessary, but should it be legislation that takes the freeze off and opens the gates wide? The freeze was put on to control freight rates. If you are going to take the freeze off you should not allow freight rates to go sky high. I agree that there should be legislation and that the freeze must eventually come off. Maybe now is the time to take it off, but if it is taken off it should be done in such a manner that there will be some degree of hesitancy on the part of the railroads to increase freight rates, and there should be some overseeing body with the authority to question and examine the necessity for any freight rate increases after the freeze is removed.
The minister's argument was weak when he said, "This surely is better than nothing." If the bill is being introduced for that reason and that reason alone, then we would be better to stick with the freeze until the minister and his officials or the transport committee can devise a new bill or proper amendments to this one to solve some of the inequities in the freight rate structure which were the cause of the MacPherson royal commission being established. This bill is born out of that commission but it solves none of the inequities of the freight rate structure other than to say that the structure is too complicated so we should throw it wide open, start all over again and see which rates go up and which are abused, and if a shipper is abused and complains loudly and proves he is being hurt by sky-rocketing freight rates we will give him a
Transportation
hearing. In some cases he will be expected to prove not only that his interest is affected but also the public interest, be it the welfare of his community or province.
This bill really does not solve the question that the commission was set up to study. It does not bring about a solution to the inequities in the freight rate structure. It does the very opposite and therefore is not the answer that the Canadian people want. The bill takes the freeze off but it is a bill and nothing more than a bill and the reasons advanced are not good enough for the house to pass it before January 1 or even by the end of January. But who knows?

Perhaps the hon. member would listen to my reply. The position I took was, I think, that there were only one or two points which I thought were being decided on second reading and one of those points was that the principle of nationalization was rejected. I am just saying now that we have had nearly two days of general debate under clause 1, and I would hope that after one or two members who are not present in the house and who 1 know wish to say something on this clause have spoken when we come back in January, we will be able to get down to the content of the bill.
As the hon. member for Comox-Albemi very properly said, apart from the broad principles of the bill, I will be quite willing to consider any reasonable amendment which I think will improve the bill, no matter which side of the house it comes from. When I say this 1 should like to add that I am pleased to say now that the suggestion made by the hon. member for Acadia about putting the word "adequate" in clause 1 to me seems to be a distinct improvement. Like him I do not care which of us moves it. I might beat him to the punch, but in any case he was the author.
Both the hon. member for Acadia and the hon. member for Qu'Appelle earlier talked about the pessimism of the MacPherson commission report and the much changed conditions since the time that report was produced. I will not be so partisan as to give any reasons for those changed conditions, but I am very glad to have the nod from the hon. member for Acadia. I was particularly cheered when the hon. member for Qu'Appelle said he believed that the prosperity was going to continue, because I really did not like the gloomy tone of the hon. member for Northumberland

who seems to be trying to talk us all into a depression again.
I do not think that anyone who has anything to do with western Canada these days can feel very depressed, because there is the kind of atmosphere in western Canada that there was when I was a boy and which unfortunately has been rather lacking through much of my adult life. I think every Canadian is very glad that this is so. I really do not think that the main purpose of the MacPherson commission was to deal with the inequities of freight rates. That was one purpose. I think the main purpose was to deal with a problem which had arisen because of the horizontal rate increases which were rolled back by the previous government at the time that commission was appointed. In order to roll them back the policy of paying subsidies to the railways was started, both in respect of the C.P.R. and the publicly owned railway. This was a new departure. To be quite fair to the previous government, I must point out that they did not say it was a policy. They said it was an expedient while a policy was being formulated.
The basic problem so far as the railways are concerned, however, is that those subsidies which started at $20 million have now reached $110 million. The subsidies which are being paid today do not take into account the new wage settlement in the railways which is approximately 24 per cent over a three-year period. Unless the railways in some way or other are permitted to improve their financial position, these funds will have to be raised somehow. They can be raised only in two ways. One source is from the shippers and the other is from the taxpayers. I think most of us in every part of the house feel that taxes are pretty high now and that we do not want to have automatic increases in taxation for specific services if those services can be made to pay for themselves.
I think it is as important to get rid of waste, inefficiency and redundancy now as it was when this was recommended by the MacPherson royal commission. It is just as important now as it was then, notwithstanding the great prosperity we have at the present time. We have to face this. We cannot forever keep putting it off.
Just as much as the hon. member for Qu'Appelle does, I regret the misunderstanding, call it what you will, about the action of the Board of Transport Commissioners. I do not think it has facilitated the passing of this bill. I think hon. members have been very

charitable with me because I think they realize that nobody was more embarrassed than I. The fact is, however, that we really must not put off forever the abandonment of lines which really are not needed, because in this way we are just making the taxpayers pay for them for very little purpose. At the same time we must make sure that we do not abandon any part of the structure which is needed or which will be needed. This is one of the things with which we have tried to deal in a constructive way, partly in this bill and partly by the government's voluntary action in undertaking to protect the great majority of the lines in western Canada. I think that action has created a much better climate in western Canada than there was before, and 1 think hon. gentlemen opposite were generous enough to say that.
[DOT] (8:10 p.m.)
That is not the only redundancy. There are services which were once important but which the railways should get rid of when there is no social advantage involved and when we have to collect taxes out of the pockets of the Canadian public to pay for them. To the extent we can get rid of redundancy and unnecessary services in order to make the railways more efficient and obtain better value for our money, we will not have to raise extra money through taxes or through increased freight rates and rates for other services.
In order to get away from the problem of ever-mounting subsidies we must rid ourselves of useless expenditures, or at least those that cannot really be justified. We must recognize that we cannot have increases in costs and wages and continue indefinitely to have static freight rates, unless the taxpayers are going to pay the bill. That is what has been happening ever since the freeze was established. We are faced with a real crisis in this regard and there is no question about that.
Up until December 31 we will have paid in the neighbourhood of $100 million because of these various freezes. We have not taken any account yet of the latest wage settlement, and I include in that statement those settlements reached through legislation and those which, happily, were settled by mediation. What are we going to do about this problem? Should we take the freeze off and allow the present law to operate?
I do not think the hon. member for Acadia understood my question to the hon. member for Winnipeg South, and I am not surprised because I sometimes do not make myself as

clear as I should. I asked the hon. member for Winnipeg South whether he would rather have the present law operate-I do not mean the freeze, because that is not the law, but a voluntary acceptance on the part of the railways of something less than the law-and let the railway companies go to the Board of Transport Commissioners to ask for a horizontal rate increase to meet increased costs and wages, or have the new bill. The freeze exists in respect of non-competitive class rates and non-competitive commodity rates. This is a large part of the spectrum where a removal of the freeze would enable the railways to apply for a horizontal or another kind of increase in respect of these non-competitive rates. In my opinion the case the railway would make for an increase in rates would be unanswerable; otherwise we have been wasting the taxpayers' money by voting these subsidies all these years. That is my point.
We are faced with this stark choice, and I do not think we have faced it squarely before now. We have three possibilities before us. We must maintain ever increasing subsidies and ever increase taxes, as we have been doing since 1958, or adopt this bill or let the present law operate. I think we have reached the end of the road of subsidies. If we continue in that

December 21, 1966
Transportation
direction the people of this country are going to rebel against the burden of taxation.
The second alternative is to follow the law as it now exists, let the railway companies go to the Board of Transport Commissioners and increase their rates wherever they can and let them apply for abandonments wherever they feel they are necessary without interference with the present law.
The third alternative is to adopt something more constructive. I think I will be successful in convincing the house that we have something more constructive in this measure. What we are saying in clause 1 of this bill is that we believe it is feasible to allow rates to be determined by competition wherever there is competition. We believe that we can rid ourselves of a great deal of regulation in this way. You may ask, what does that mean? It makes a lot of difference. Thousands of man-hours in the form of very expensive labour, such as the services of Dr. Bandeen, are wasted every year in hearings before the Board of Transport Commissioners and dealing with unnecessary regulations. We feel strongly that we should not regulate things that need not be regulated. If we can protect the public, both shippers and consumers, by competition without having a whole lot of bureaucrats measuring the rules and interpreting them we will save a great deal of money.
One of the difficulties regarding competitive rates is that though during the freeze competitive rates could be increased, so much notice was required that other transport companies could often under-cut the competitive rates. We want to give the railway companies an opportunity to compete in competitive areas. We believe there is so much regulation now that these companies do not have the opportunity of operating as competitively as possible. I personally believe that railway companies can obtain far more revenue from competitive areas if they are allowed to compete. If they get more revenue from these areas they will not have the necessity to charge such high rates in non-competitive areas. This will result in more equitable freight rates for non-competitive areas.
The hon. gentleman asked whether the C.P.R. and the C.N.R. compete for business. Surely each of us judges that for himself and forms some ideas. There are more ways of competing for business than by rates. Even in areas where there is no alternative mode of transport, wherever two railway companies provide a service customers will go to both to see which one will give the best rate.

[DOT] (8:20 p.m4
That fact leads me to a point raised yesterday by the hon. member for Medicine Hat and another hon. member who raised the same point. They seemed to assume that, in some way or other, the railways under the law can set secret rates to favour one customer over another. There is no way whatever under the present law that the railways can lawfully set any secret rate. Every rate the railways charge any customer is, by law, available for inspection. I know a number of hon. members, particulary hon. members from Saskatchewan, Alberta and Manitoba, are very worried about the situation of the shippers of bulk commodities who obviously have no other way to ship except by rail. Therefore in that sense, not in the special sense of this bill, they are captive shippers. In other words, they have no other place to go than to the railways.
For almost all commodities many shippers have access to both railways. Once one of the railways has set a rate that is acceptable and has been published, under clause 16 any shipper who is charged a higher rate under similar geographical circumstances, similar circumstances of volume and so on, will have a grievance. He will have a grievance if he is charged a higher rate and it will be against the public interest to charge it. That is what the clause says. I think the hon. member for Winnipeg South did not thoroughly appreciate the fact that this clause was very substantially modified compared with the earlier provisions of the bill, the proposed section 317.
The modifications were based mainly upon the representations made by the government of Manitoba and it seemed to me they met the point fairly precisely. I believe that clause 16 has pretty well accomplished what many members hoped would be accomplished, and which would never be accomplished by a maximum rate formula such as there is in section 336. The purpose of the maximum rate formula is to protect the relatively small shippers, who at the present time, have to pay class rates. We have tried and have not been able to find any way to devise a maximum rate formula that would provide anything like reasonable revenues for the railways on small shipments that now go by class rates and would fit the circumstances of bulk shippers who now have commodity rates. Unless we are going to go right back into the field of complicated regulations, which we are trying to get away from, I do not believe it can be done. I say this because some of the best experts I have been able to find have tried
December 21, 198$

very hard and in various ways to find such a formula. I just do not think it can be devised.
I think there is far more protection of the kind that is really needed in the new clause 16 for commodity shippers than any kind of maximum rate formula that could possibly be devised. But we do need the maximum rate formula to protect the small shipper. I was rather interested that Dr. Bortz in his evidence before the committee indicated that under his calculations as well as he could make them, the shipper shipping small quantities would, under the maximum rate formula, in a substantial number of cases have a lower rate than he is now paying under the class rates. So it does appear to offer some reasonable measure of protection to the only kind of shipper that in my view a maximum rate formula can protect. The improved clause 16 will, I think, provide the protection needed to shippers of bulk commodities.
I should now like to deal with the question of the public interest. The public interest is not circumscribed, but there are certain things that are definitely said not to be in the public interest. The most important of these is found in subclause (3) of clause 16 on page 9 of the bill:
In conducting an investigation under this section, the Commission shall have regard to all considerations that appear to it to be relevant-
In other words, the commission may say that anything that seems to it to be relevant is part of the public interest.
-including, without limiting the generality of the foregoing,
(a) whether the tolls or conditions specified for the carriage of traffic under the rate so established are such as to create an unfair disadvantage beyond that which may be deemed to be inherent in the location or volume of the traffic, the scale of operation connected therewith or the type of traffic or service involved:
That really means that if you are shipping from roughly the same geographic area to the same point, say on the coast, and are shipping at roughly the same volume, it is against the public interest to charge one shipper a different rate from another shipper. That is said quite specifically in this bill to be against the public interest. I think it would also clearly be against the public interest for a railway to seek to charge a rate which would in fact be so high as to make it impossible for a shipper to export who already had established himself and had had a rate previously, so long, of course, as a lower rate was compensatory, because that is one of the other requirements of the bill. We are saying that the railways
23033-728J
Transportation
are not permitted to charge rates that are not compensatory, except in certain specified cases where the treasury will make up the difference. When you take all these geographical and other factors into account and take the fact that there are two railways, to which certain hon. gentlemen object but which I think provides a quite considerable protection to shippers, it seems to me there is in clause 16 a pretty adequate protection, about as effective a protection as can be devised.
There seems to be-I do not think it is explicit at all-an implicit assumption that in some way or other the government is anxious to get railway rates higher than they need to be. I have to be elected. All my colleagues have to be elected. The members on this side of the house who are supporting the government have to be elected. They are not going to get many votes by giving the railways higher rates than they need. They are much more apt to get votes by any protective device that will keep the rates down. At the same time, we are not likely to continue to get public support for very long if we keep the rates down by dishing out endless subsidies and then bringing in increases in income tax and sales taxes to pay for them. This is the problem. If it were an easy problem to solve it would have been solved long ago. It would have been solved by the previous government without ever appointing the MacPherson royal commission. It would have been solved during all these years in between. It has not been solved.
[DOT] (8:30 p.m.)
It is just about as difficult and intractable an economic and social problem as one could think of. I do suggest that, although there may still be some improvements and refinements, as a result of the conscientious work of the committee, based on what I like to think was a pretty good framework to start with, we have the makings of a good piece of legislation which, however, cannot be absolutely perfect. That is why we have made two or three provisions for statutory reviews of these procedures, because we know they are not going to be perfect and we know they will have to be improved in the light of experience. But I doubt that we will get a very much better bill by taking another six months at it. I certainly agree that we need a few more days.
I am disappointed, as are the hon. gentlemen opposite who are so sympathetic to me, but everybody knows that I really have been pushed around terribly by my colleagues. I am the low man on the totem pole. I admit

Transportation

subtopic: PROVISION FOR DEFINITION AND IMPLEMENTATION OF NATIONAL POLICY
speechtext: I think the hon. gentleman has left out what I believe is the most important element of all. Before we consider increasing the subsidies or setting higher rates there are two other things which should be done first. The second thing is to give the railways a chance to get more business by enabling them to compete more actively for the traffic and to do so in a more businesslike way so that by getting more business at the existing rates they can improve their financial position and as a result will not have to raise their rates so much. First of all, I do not think it possible to have one rate structure for the Canadian Pacific Railway, to which the hon. gentleman's remarks applied, and an entirely different one for the Canadian National Railways. The companies which form the Canadian National Railways were also given a lot of the public domain to build the railways. They dissipated those assets and went broke. They were taken over by the government during the first world war and afterwards, and in my view they are publicly owned, though the hon. member for Timiskaming in an extraordnary kind of convoluted argument this afternoon seemed to suggest they were not publicly owned. At any rate they have been a tremendous drain on the treasury for a very long time.
There is no doubt that one could say to the Canadian Pacific Railway, because you have been provident when all the other private railways were improvident, because you made good use of the assets you had when Canadian Northern, Grand Truck Pacific and all the others dissipated theirs you should therefore take the revenue from all these assets into account and because you make so much out of Consolidated Mining and Smelting and other investments of that sort you can afford to give the Canadian people free service, or practically free service, on your railway. If they did that, wherever there was any competition, the Canadian National would get no traffic at all.
Transportation
This is one of the practical difficulties of this concept.
The Solicitor General will correct me if I am wrong about this but I understand that the courts have determined why the grants were made to the Canadian Pacific Railway. They agreed to build the railway if they got these concessions. A great many other Canadians received concessions out of the public domain in the 19th century for doing other things, but to my knowledge nobody has suggested they should provide their services at an uneconomic rate because either by good fortune, good luck or good managment they made the most of their assets.
If the Canadian Pacific were really the kind of soulless corporation it is customary to protray it as in political speeches, this problem would not be so difficult. We could say that they could take their revenues from their assets and run their railway at a loss because they are making so much out of other things. However, one must remember that Lord Mount Stephen, Lord Strathcona and Sir William Van Horne are all dead. Even Lord Shaughnessy and Sir Edward Beatty are dead. The securities of the C.P.R. have changed hands hundreds of times.
If we told the C.P.R. that they had to provide their services at a loss and derive all their revenues from these other companies, I can just see the Leader of the Opposition talking about the widows and orphans who own C.P.R. stock and how the Minister of Finance ought to compensate them for the shocking injustice being done to them by the public. The tears we have seen him weep would be nothing in comparison, and the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre would not be far behind.
I have tried to avoid controversial subjects like this and like icebreaking on the St. Lawrence, where if you say something pleasing to one part of the country it is sure to displease another part. I am like the hon. member for Trois-Rivieres, rather naive and simpleminded. There are times when I find it a little hard to perpetuate the old-fashioned hypocrisies in which no one really believes but which in politics we so often repeat over and over again.
The other day in Halifax I took my life in my hands, politically speaking, when I said I would not do anything to prevent the development of navigation on the St. Lawrence, that we were taking no extraordinary measures to accelerate it but would not do anything to prevent it. Five years ago if any politician had

said that in Halifax he could not have got out of the city fast enough. Perhaps the junior member for Halifax is naive too, but he said I was fairly well received there.
The plain fact is that once in a while we have to face the realities of public life. Whether or not it was wise to give the C.P.R. 25 million acres of land, whether or not Sir John Macdonald, who is also dead, made a great mistake in doing this, we cannot undo it now. Whether or not it was wise to give this grant to build a railway I am not going to say. When I leave this place and return to a university to lecture in history I will give my opinion on this question, but I will not do so today.
Nevertheless this is a fact of our political life and the consequences that flow from that fact are with us. There is no practical way I can see of solving this problem simply by saying to the Canadian Pacific Railway that they have to undo all that has been done in the past, treat the revenues from all these other assets as though they were railway revenues and run the railway as a kind of public charity. The minister said a little earlier: Because the C.P.R. has been given generous concessions and has displayed an intelligent and objective administration, should we take that as an excuse to beg that company for low rates? There was no mention of this, when the Canadian Pacific Railways were established, and all these concessions were made. Would it not be advisable to clarify the situation today and make an appraisal of all that has been granted to the C.P.R.? As for those who later became millionaires and have since left us for a better world, I hope the Almighty is watching over them, because I do not want to trouble their eternal rest or that of their heirs. Nevertheless, I feel that when Canada granted them certain privileges, natural resources and operating rights, Canada was not entering into a ten, 20 or 50 year contract, but rather a contract which was to last as long as our country should survive. As for those who made millions with these concessions, it is not our worry whether they be in Heaven or elsewhere.

Our problem is whether the company, originally called Canadian Pacific Railways, which has since subdivided its operations to find out which would make millions and which would be in the red, thereby being subsidized by Canada, our problem, as I say, is whether we should not now make a re-appraisal and say: You have been conceded much up to now, but it is necessary that we should establish some common denominator in order to ascertain whether you should give back to Canada what it gave to you. And this, to a certain extent and taking into account the fact that such enterprises should bring in some profits, some dividends, certain advantages which we have no objection to.
I am not talking about nationalizing railways. I am for private enterprise as much as possible, at least just as long as contingencies

do not require otherwise. But I am one of those who, through simple-mindedness or candour, is a little surprised to see that the C.P.R. was given everything to start with and that subtle questions were not asked as to what would be economic and what would not, and that in 1966-67 the C.P.R. should say to us: well, railways, airlines, hotels and mines are all economic and we will keep them-I do not know, I am not familiar enough with the whole organization to make an objective analysis-but passenger service is not; therefore, let the government take it over or subsidize it. Well, there is something wrong here. An agreement was made with the C.P.R., tremendous advantages were conceded. I realize that the C.P.R. ran some risks at the time, but history has now proved that there have been ample rewards for the risks that were taken.
Should not the Canadian people today, who, after all, own those natural resources and those rights we have granted them, be justified to say: Give us a balance-sheet, showing what this has brought you up to now and what you have contributed to this country? Mr. Chairman, we know that the Canadian Pacific cannot be taxed by the municipalities on its main line in western Canada. That is part of the contract of 1881 and that contractual right is part of the constitution of Canada at the moment, I regret to say. At least, the lawyers say it is. The Canadian Pacific Railway was built pursuant to a contract between the government of Canada and the Canadian Pacific Railway in 1881, if I remember correctly. The first statute of the session of 1881 was a statute confirming that contract.
It is true of course that this parliament is sovereign and we can abrogate any contract we like with or without compensation. That is the theory on which our constitution rests. But it has been the custom of all governments of Canada up to the present time to respect contracts into which governments have entered even if sometimes they were improvident contracts. I was speaking quite seriously a little while ago when I said that whether that contract originally was provident or improvident, it is a contract and it has to be construed by the courts. We can make a law saying that the contract is abrogated. Except in the one respect I have mentioned, I do not know of any other respect in which we could not abrogate it unilaterally. But we just do not do that kind of thing. We never have up to now and we have never had a government or parliament willing to do that.
If the Canadian Pacific is not carrying out that contract, if it is doing anything to divest itself of certain of its assets which is illegal, then of course we should make the C.P.R. obey the law. There is no question about that in my mind. If they are doing something that is against public policy we can make a law to stop it. I think perhaps that is where I would not disagree much with the hon. gentleman. If the Canadian Pacific is rearranging its assets in such a way as to be contrary to good public policy-I am not saying whether it is or is not because it is not a question I have studied-if it is rearranging its assets in such a way, and I know that there are many people who think it is and some people think strongly that it is not, then it would be an appropriate subject for this parliament to deal with and correct.

But I think there are other things that we sometimes forget. When they got those 25 million acres in 1881, most people said the land

was not worth anything. In the period after 1881, and particularly after 1896 and indeed up to the time my father homesteaded between the lakes in Manitoba in 1911, you could get a quarter section of land for five bucks. The land was free. You filed on the land and then you had to clear so many acres over three years and then you could get a patent and it was yours.
In some cases those lands turned out to have tremendously valuable minerals on them. In some cases they did not. As the hon. member for Humboldt-Melfort-Tisdale knows as well as I do, homesteading was a lottery. But we have never said that the fellow who struck it rich has got to give it back, except to the extent anybody else does who makes money any other way, in ordinary taxes. This has gone on all over western Canada. It is not only the C.P.R. which have received grants of land.
I think we would have to look at that problem as a whole, deal with one case compared with another and do similar justice to all. Otherwise I think we would be creating a very serious injustice which would be visited upon people who had no original responsibility for the situation. But I certainly agree that to the extent that the hon. gentleman was able to show, or that anyone else was able to show, that the Canadian Pacific Railway Company was arranging its affairs and assets in a way that was contrary to public policy, in other words, that it was really milking the railway, so to speak, and particularly if we were paying subsidies at the same time, then that would be something that certainly should be corrected. I understand it has been construed several times in the courts and, unless we change the law, as the courts have construed it, it remains the law.

speechtext: While copies of this bill are being distributed perhaps I could say a word or two as a member of the standing committee which considered this measure. In its present form the bill is not sufficient in its application in so far as members of this party are concerned. As the minister has suggested it did receive thorough study in a committee of the other place as well as in the standing committee of this house. While we regret that our amendments were not supported by a majority of this house we are satisfied to allow the passage of the bill without extended discussion. We are prepared to allow the minister and his department to have a whirl at this measure in its present form. We may have some further remarks to make about it at a future date in respect of how it could be improved. The bill in its present form represents a constructive step in the field of safety for employees of this country, and we are appreciative of the fact that the proposal was brought forward at this time.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. L. B. Pearson (Prime Minister):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise on a question of privilege. It is a very real privilege to be able, as the leader of the government, to wish all hon. members here the compliments of the season.
I feel that I am wishing these compliments to a gallant band of survivors who have resisted the temptation to fly home prematurely and have even resisted the temptation to stay out in the lobby and watch a hockey game on television. It has been a long and hard session. In our own ways, and they have not always been the same ways, we have done our best to make it a productive session in the best interests and welfare of the people of our country.
I think we have earned a Merry Christmas. I hope we will deserve a Happy New Year.
Hear, hear.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, we wish to thank the right hon. Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) for his good wishes and the hope that we have a happy new year. I do not think the new year can be very prosperous in view of all the taxes with which we have been saddled and with which we expect to be further saddled in the next budget to be brought down. However, in all sincerity we wish to reciprocate the Prime Minister's good wishes and say to him and his colleagues that we wish them a very merry Christmas.
Hear, hear.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, on behalf of the New Democratic Party may I express our thanks to the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) for the good wishes he has extended. We are very happy to reciprocate those good wishes to the Prime Minister, and we convey them also to the members of the government and to all hon. members of all parties in this House of Commons. We would like also to extend our special greetings to you, sir, as our first commoner-
Hear, hear.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
speechtext: -to the other occupants of the chair, to those at the table, the staff, the page boys, and because it is Christmas I might even include the press. We join in the sentiments the Prime Minister has expressed. We trust we may all have a merry Christmas and that our work in the coming months will make it a happier new year for the Canadian people.
Hear, hear.

Mr. Speaker, first of all, I should like to express to you and to the right hon. Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) the heartfelt admiration of our group. We offer you our best wishes for a long and happy life.
We extend the same wishes also to all the hon. members of this house, to all those who worked to make Canada a better country and give it better legislation and a higher standard of living.
Last year, I said that I would do my best to convince the house to increase family allowances. I have not won my point, but
December 21, 1966

I hope that 1967 will be a year of achievements and that family allowances will be increased, so that every family may benefit from its share of the technical, scientific and other progress achieved, and everything to which families are entitled.
I express the wish that each and every Canadian family will enjoy a better standard of living all through 1967 and share in the growth of production that we will have again in 1967, because Canada is developing and going ahead. Moreover, if such development occurs in Canada, it must also be reflected in each family and in each home, because every individual should get his share.
Such is the wish I make, saying thank you to everyone and wishing a Merry Christmas to all.
[DOT] (9:40 p.m.)

Mr. Speaker, on behalf of the Social Credit group I would like to express our appreciation to the right hon. Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) for his words of greetings and best wishes. We also wish to convey our good wishes to the right hon. gentlemen, to the government, to you, sir, and to every member of the house.
In the past weeks and months we have witnessed acrimonius debates which may not have been conducive to a happy Christmas, but I am sure that now that we have drawn close to the time of the year when we remember the birth of the Prince of Peace we will all join in some soul-searching which will help us when we return to carry out our responsibilities in a pleasing and satisfactory manner.

Mr. Speaker, on behalf of my small group, I wish to thank the right hon. Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) for his good wishes and I wish to extend to him and his party, and also to every member of this house, my best wishes for a happy and prosperous year 1967.
Obviously, 1967 will be a very important year for Canada. Indeed, we will be celebrating our first centennial and we will play host to a world exhibition.
In this our centennial year, may all Canadians, from sea to sea, finally realize that national harmony and brotherhood cannot flourish in this country unless everyone receives fair and equal treatment.
Christmas Adjournment
And, in connection with the world exhibition, may all foreign visitors to our country feel with us that we are part of a single and great family here on earth and realize that we must all work to banish war from this earth and love one another as individuals and as a people, true to the teachings of the Divine Child, from the day he was born in the manger and throughout his whole life.
